# The Kraken Mare Light

On Titan's Kraken Mare, where liquid methane barges cross a black sea under a nitrogen sky, Marit Anselm is the last human keeper the Mare Authority still funds — and the decommissioning notice on her station has thirty days left to run. Then a distress bundle arrives speaking in her own voice, reporting a ballast failure she never called in. The custody stamps say it was composed nine years ago, relayed through a buoy the Authority's own records list as dead. She has never filed a false report in her life. She is not about to start believing in ghosts.

What she finds instead is worse: a voiceprint beacon does not lie, and neither does a bundle's timestamped chain of custody — which means somewhere in the tholin-fouled dark, a message that should never have moved has started moving again, and the people who signed off on it staying silent for nine years are the same people about to decide whether her station, and her purpose, still matter. Between a freight guild running illegal shortcuts, a salvage crew that treats silence as ownership, and an auditor whose signature closed the case the first time, Anselm has three days and a failing power budget to find out who is really speaking through that beacon, and what waited nine years to be heard.

For readers of *The Expanse*, *Blindsight*, and *Version Control*, this is hard-vacuum procedural at its most exacting — a mystery where the physics is the alibi.
# Chapter 1 — Custody Stamp 2138

The tholin came off the radar dome in flakes the colour of old tobacco, and Marit Anselm scraped at it with the edge of a nylon spatula because metal scratched the radome and a scratched radome scattered. Ninety-four kelvin. Four hours on the suit clock, two remaining before the heaters lost their argument with the nitrogen. The wind pushed at her back, thick and slow, the way a crowd pushes.

Inside, out of the shell, she logged the work nobody would read. Behind her on the board, thirty days old and unanswered, Corvin Ladd's decommissioning audit notice glowed its patient argument: *the buoy chain can carry custody unaided.*

The short-range link chimed at 0412 station time. A distress bundle, inbound off the buoy chain, flagged for custodial acknowledgement within one relay window.

She opened it and her own voice came out of the speaker.

Not a recording. Synthesis — the flat Authority cadence of a voiceprint beacon — but her vowels, the way she shortened the *a* in *ballast*, and the small dry catch in the throat before a hard consonant that she had been told about at nineteen and had never once managed to hear in herself. It said: *Ballast seal on the aft tank is going. Rate is increasing. I am setting the pumps to full and I do not expect it to be enough. Position is Nicholson Shoal, bearing—*

The words were plain and ordered and someone else's. She had never said them. She had never been in Nicholson Shoal in a pod with a failing tank. The voice was hers the way a fingerprint on a glass is yours after you have put the glass down.

Duplicate fault, she typed. Beacon echo, source unresolved. Filed.

Then she opened the custody chain, because a bundle carries the signed timestamps of every node that ever held it, and bundles cannot be forged or deleted, only delayed.

Composed 2138.

She read it four times and it did not change, because it could not. The origin stamp was nine years old and the custody stamp under it belonged to Buoy 47 — a node written off, a node the Authority's own tables listed as dead and left floating wherever it had drifted. After that, every stamp was Buoy 47 again, and none of them older than thirty days. After that, Buoy 47 again, and again, and again, the chain doubling back through the same dead node for nine years, and not one stamp in it older than thirty days. She scrolled to the bottom and back to the top. It was not possible and it was signed. She wrote no theory down.

She went at it sideways, because the front of it was a wall. She pulled her own radar track for the past week and laid it against the Kraken Freight Guild's filed weather. Seven days back: the *Sorrel Draught*, barge master Oyuna Brecht, cutting a line straight through Nicholson Shoal on a sea state her filing did not justify. Marit noted it, without knowing what it was worth, the way you note a number before you know it is the answer.

At 0631 the link chimed again.

The same voice. Her voice. And the custody stamps were four days old.
# Chapter 2 — Dead Node, Live Signature

The registration record came up off the local store, no uplink needed: 2131, her thumbprint, her voiceprint sampled in a warm room at Station 7, and beneath it the custody signature for survey pod Wick-3. Permanent and non-transferable. Marit Anselm read the clause twice, the way she read fault codes, looking for the interpretation that let her stop.

There wasn't one. The beacon in Wick-3 had been speaking in her voice since before it sank, because the Authority had decided once that a rescuer should hear a person and not a tone. The registered wearer that winter was Halvard Ness. The words were his. He had composed them while the pod went under on a re-anchoring run she had ordered.

She walked the custody stamps backwards, hop by hop, and found the place where the chain stopped being a chain. Buoy 47, 2138, custody accepted. After that, nothing — no handoff, no acknowledgement, only the buoy's own re-transmit stamps, a thirty-day cache refusing to let go because nothing had ever told it the message was delivered. Its uplink horn was tholin-fouled. It could hear. It could not be heard. For nine years it had rebroadcast into an empty arc, out of every line of sight on Kraken Mare, re-signing its own custody each cycle like a man repeating a sentence to keep from forgetting it.

She overlaid the buoy's drift on the *Sorrel Draught*'s real track, not the filed one. Oyuna Brecht's anchor had fouled the derelict eight days ago and dragged it roughly fourteen kilometres east — inside the seventeen-kilometre horizon of a sixty-metre mast. The network had been repaired by accident, by a crime.

Delphine Sarr sold her uplink seconds at the posted rate and not one kilobit of courtesy. Anselm spent them on the 2139 inquest evidence list. What came back, three passes later, was not testimony but a query filter: *node classes excluded — dead*. Nobody had read Buoy 47's log, because a buoy that has never handed off a bundle reports as dead.

On the open distress band, thin through the drizzle static, Tomas Weir's cooperative logged the same unanswered call and timed it. Seventy-two hours, and the beacon became abandoned property. She was not the only listener.

The last thing she did took an hour and killed the hope. The fresh stamps were genuine — new emissions, every forty minutes, from Wick-3's radioisotope beacon, still fed, still patient, one hundred eighty metres down in five hundred kilograms per cubic metre of methane-ethane.

A failed seal at ninety-four kelvin kills by conduction in under ninety seconds. The pod's tank had gone in 2138.

Halvard Ness died in 2138. Nothing down there was alive. The machine had simply kept its promise for nine years, and she had been nine years out of earshot.
# Chapter 3 — Nine Minutes a Pass

She spent the heaters first, because the heaters were hers to spend.

Nine minutes a pass, three passes running: seven kilowatts drawn against a five-kilowatt plant, the battery bank sagging, the habitat browning out from the walls inward. Marit Anselm worked in her liner with her hands going stiff and the cold arriving the way everything on Titan arrived, from the edges and late. Uplink one carried the custodial acknowledgement of a distress bundle composed in 2138. Uplink two carried the custody chain entire — every stamp Buoy 47 had laid on it for nine years, unhandoffed, unread. Uplink three carried the fix.

The fix she got on day four. Buoy 47's stamps were a position log nobody had asked to read: each one a timestamp against a drift the buoy had not chosen. She laid them over Oyuna Brecht's real track through Nicholson Shoal — not the filed weather, the track — and ran the drag vector backwards ten days to the point where the anchor had first fouled the derelict. One hundred eighty metres of methane-ethane under it. She could defend that fix to a metre, and she wrote down how, twice.

Corvin Ladd's answer came back through the Ligeia Head dish by way of the Authority's Earth office, which meant eighty-some minutes out and eighty-some minutes home, a lag he could not shorten and had not tried to. A one-sided voice that had stopped speaking before she heard a word of it.

He did not deny the filter. He explained it. Dead nodes excluded from the audit set; a buoy that has never handed off reports dead; and a transmitting beacon meant a chain that swallowed distress traffic, and that finding would have frozen eighteen station retirements. *Not a conspiracy,* he said, into the hour and a half between them. *An incentive. And a default.*

Tomas Weir took the coordinates for a lift, because the arithmetic was honest and he was scrupulous about custom. His cooperative raised *Wick-3* intact on day four, seals unbroken where they had not broken, the whole of it preserved unchanged at ninety-four kelvin, and gave up its author. Halvard Ness, nine years dead, steady on the record. The text was still in the beacon's buffer in his own composition, plainspoken, ordered, finished. Her voice had been saying his words since before she was censured for the silence.

The acknowledgement she had bought with her heaters became the Authority's proof that the chain could hold a distress bundle nine years with no human to notice it. That was the charter clause exactly. Ladd's audit reversed on the evidence Ladd's audit had provoked. Station 12 stayed crewed, which meant she stayed.

Vindication and sentence in one signature. She brought the heaters up, sat back at the console, and logged the next acknowledgement nobody would read. Saturn was where it had been.
